articles.title_zh: China Warns US on New Chip Export Controls
articles.content_orig:
Editorial · CASRAI · Research security
China’s foreign ministry said on November 13, 2026 it opposes the abuse of export controls as US lawmakers push for tighter chip limits.

On Friday, November 13, 2026, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a regular press briefing that China “has consistently opposed the abuse of export control measures,” which she said “serves no party’s interests.” She was responding to calls from US lawmakers for tighter limits on chip-equipment exports to China, as reported by CBS News (with AFP) .
According to the CBS/AFP report, Mao urged both countries to implement the consensus reached by their heads of state and to maintain “the stable development of China-U.S. economic and trade relations.” The report does not describe a specific new rule; the remarks answered statements from members of Congress rather than a published regulation.
A day earlier, on Thursday, Beijing described spy allegations linked to the Nvidia affair as a “pretext for imposing a technological blockade” aimed at halting China’s AI advances, the same report says.
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting an affair, reportedly with a former senior executive at the Singapore data-centre firm Megaspeed, CBS reports. The New York Times reported that US officials had circulated a memo alleging that executive was a Chinese intelligence operative. See our earlier coverage: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns; Colette Kress named interim CEO .
House Speaker Mike Johnson said Congress is increasingly united behind tighter chip export controls on China, according to the same report. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CNBC that Commerce had not added Megaspeed to the Entity List, noting “Commerce BIS has the pen.” A US official said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 10. For the oversight track, see Senate Banking summons Lutnick and Huang over AI chip probe , and for the legislative proposal on remote access, US senators urge tighter licensing for remote access to AI chips .
Nothing in the Chinese statement changes US law today. It is a diplomatic position on proposals that are still being discussed, and the CBS report does not identify a pending bill or rule text. Its practical value for a university is as a signal about the direction of the policy environment. These are editorial interpretations, not findings from the report:
The next concrete markers are the Senate Banking hearing, reported for December 10, any bill or Commerce rule text on chip-equipment controls, and whether the two governments make further statements about implementing the consensus reached by their leaders. Until rule text exists, offices should treat the situation as one to monitor rather than act on.

articles.title_orig: Trump to meet Xi, Putin in historic three-way talks in China on November 19
articles.title_zh: Trump to meet Xi, Putin in historic three-way talks in China on November 19
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Donald Trump will meet Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China next week for an unprecedented three-way meeting between the leaders of the US , Russia , and China, with nuclear weapons and the war in Iran expected to be on the agenda.
The meeting will take place on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, the White House confirmed on Friday. It will bring together the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers for the first time, although all three have held bilateral talks with one another.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The meeting comes nine months after the expiry of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), the last major nuclear arms control agreement between Washington and Moscow.
The treaty, which expired in February, had placed limits on the two countries’ strategic nuclear arsenals, leaving the world’s two largest nuclear powers without those restrictions for the first time in more than half a century.
Mr Trump has rejected Russia's offer to extend it for another year, saying he wanted a new agreement that would also include China.
Beijing has resisted joining such negotiations, arguing that its nuclear arsenal is much smaller than those of Washington and Moscow. China has more than 600 nuclear warheads, compared with more than 5,000 each for Russia and the US.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told reporters, according to Reuters. “This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think ​it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have ​adult conversations about adult things.”
Mr Trump also intends to discuss the war in Iran with Mr Xi and Mr Putin, but Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is not expected to feature, the official said. “We’ve had many meetings ⁠recently with ​the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, ​so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official said.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly insisted that his country must be involved in any discussions about its future.
Russia had previously proposed the three-way meeting, with Mr Putin reportedly keen to use it to discuss Ukraine. The Russian president had floated the idea during a telephone conversation with Trump last month, according to the Wall Street Journal .
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha had warned against giving Putin such a platform. “Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandisement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” he said last month, adding that it would only “encourage Putin to continue this war”.
The planned summit has also drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union discussed the postwar settlement in Europe. The prospect of Mr Trump, Mr Putin, and Mr Xi meeting without Ukraine has revived concerns about major powers making decisions that affect other countries without consulting them.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the comparison, saying that any agreements reached in Shenzhen could not be imposed on other countries. He nevertheless described a meeting between the three leaders as “extremely significant”. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect,” he said.
Mr Trump is due to visit Manila on Tuesday for talks with leaders of the Association of South-east Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen. He is also scheduled to hold bilateral talks and a working lunch with Xi on Thursday, ahead of the trilateral meeting.
The White House said billionaire Elon Musk would accompany Mr Trump on the China visit, but a senior US official said he would not attend the talks with Mr Xi and Mr Putin.

articles.title_orig: Russell Brand: Alleged rape victim wants age of consent law changed
articles.title_zh: Russell Brand: Alleged rape victim wants age of consent law changed
articles.content_orig:
Deputy prime minister says change would be a massive step but ‘deserves proper consideration and scrutiny’
The government has said it will consider calls to change the age of consent after a woman waived her right to anonymity to publicly claim she was raped by Russell Brand as a 16-year-old schoolgirl.
Mia Latter, now 37, alleged she had been orally raped by the jailed comedian when she was a teenager and he was 30 years old.
In an interview with the Sunday Times, she called for the introduction of a staggered age of consent – which would make relationships between adults and teenagers aged 16 and 17 illegal.
Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, told the newspaper that Latter’s “heart-breaking story” meant a law change deserved consideration.
She said: “We need to listen to Mia and other victims like her who have been through these experiences because it’s really important that as lawmakers their experience is at the heart of what we consider.
“It clearly would be a massive step to change the age of consent, but it deserves proper consideration and scrutiny. I can absolutely understand why she is calling for it.”
Under UK law, adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds.
Latter said: “It’s shocking to me time and time again that whenever the news comes up again about him, it’s always in the comments about the relationship with a 16-year-old.
“That’s not the most heinous bit. But why is that the thing that everybody collectively gets stuck on? I think we all sort of agree that … adults shouldn’t be allowed to have sexual relationships with children, with somebody under the age of 18. That really doesn’t seem like a gigantic leap to take.”
Latter was referred to under the pseudonym of Alice in previous reporting by the Sunday Times, the Times, and Channel 4’s Dispatches documentary.
She was 16 when she first met Brand in Leicester Square, central London, while she was on her way home from a shopping trip.
He took her number and later messaged her, asking if she wanted to go for dinner, she said.
She told the newspaper that Brand – who was working at MTV at the time – still asked her to meet after she had confessed her age to him.
Latter alleges Brand orally raped her towards the end of their three-month relationship.
Brand denied all of the allegations made against him by Latter when they were first reported in 2023 by the Times.
She spoke to the police after the documentary, but the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) decided not to include her case in Brand’s trial at Southwark Crown Court.
He was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him, and is now serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term for one count of rape and three sexual assaults.
Earlier this week, it was announced that a series of “serious” sex offence allegations against comedian David Walliams are being probed by the Metropolitan police after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News.
One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”.
Walliams denies any wrongdoing.
Haigh went on to say that, in light of news that one of Walliams’s accusers was asked to sign a non disclosure agreement (NDA), the government should also look at banning them in cases of alleged sexual assault and harassment. She said: “When we consider the allegations against David Walliams, teenagers who were fans wouldn’t come under the current consultation.
“I do think there is a very strong case to look at banning NDAs in all circumstances where they relate to harassment or discrimination, to make sure that no victim, regardless of where it happened or what their relationship was with the perpetrator, should ever be silenced.”
It is believed MPs outside Labour may support a bill to change the age of consent laws, with Jess Brown-Fuller, the Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson, coming out in favour of reviewing them.
Commending Latter for the “extraordinary bravery” it took to waive her anonymity, Brown-Fuller said: “I think we must go further to increase protections for young women and girls, and looking at a staggered age of consent is an important step.
“We already have rules that recognise power imbalances in professions: between teachers and students, or barristers and junior colleagues. It’s time for the government to recognise the implicit power imbalance held by older men over teenage girls.”
Latter’s decision to come forward was also praised by Bridget Phillipson, the minister for women and equalities, who said she “and thousands of others across the country will be in awe of her courage and determination”. She added that it is “up to all of us to send a message to women and girls who experience sexual violence: the shame is not yours. Women like Mia are leading the charge, but we can and must do more to make this a moment of change.”
Latter’s allegation was reported to the Met police, who said the investigation into the alleged rape remains ongoing.
A Met Police spokesperson said: “Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape.
“Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made.
“This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence.”
The CPS said: “The Crown Prosecution Service will continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible.”

Ukraine ’s president Volodymyr Zelensky has accused SpaceX of hampering his country’s defences by maintaining speed restrictions on its Starshield satellite terminals in Russian-occupied territory. The limits, which Ukraine says have been in place for five days, are making it harder for its forces to intercept Russian jet-powered drones before they reach Ukrainian cities.
Zelensky dismissed the company's explanation that the restrictions were caused by a “technical issue”, telling reporters on Saturday: “We do not believe that is the case.”
He warned that limiting the service in occupied territory carried political implications, adding: “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporarily occupied territories as not ours.”
SpaceX has denied imposing restrictions or changing its satellite operations.
Zelensky also revealed that US negotiators had asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from Donbas in exchange for Nato membership during talks in Abu Dhabi. “This was the first time this had been raised,” he said, insisting Kyiv would not surrender its territory.
Russia has claimed that its forces struck a cargo vessel and port infrastructure in Chornomorsk, in Ukraine’s Odesa region, on Saturday.
The Russian defence ministry said the vessel was being used to transport supplies for the Ukrainian military and that facilities used to unload military cargo had also been hit, according to state news agency RIA Novosti.
US negotiators have asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for joining Nato, president Zelensky has said.
“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelensky told reporters on Saturday.
He insisted Kyiv was not prepared to surrender its territory, but said he would put the question to a national referendum if Ukraine received a comprehensive security package, including firm guarantees, a strong and properly funded military, and money for reconstruction.
Zelensky said the proposal meant Nato membership was “back on the agenda”, but acknowledged that reaching an agreement would be difficult given Vladimir Putin’s opposition to Ukraine joining the alliance.
Volodymyr Zelensky has accused SpaceX of maintaining speed restrictions on Starshield, its military-focused satellite communications system, saying they are leaving Ukrainian forces less able to intercept Russian drones.
The restrictions have been in place for five days, with terminals in Russian-occupied territory capped at 161km/h, he said.
“We do not believe that is the case," Zelensky told reporters on Saturday, rejecting SpaceX’s explanation that the problem was technical.
He also warned that restricting the service in occupied territory amounted to partially recognising those areas as no longer Ukrainian. “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” he said.
Ukraine’s envoy in Washington Denys Sienik told RFE that the restrictions were widespread. SpaceX has denied making any changes to its service.

articles.title_orig: Saudi-led coalition intercepts suspected Houthi missiles and drones
articles.title_zh: Saudi-led coalition intercepts suspected Houthi missiles and drones
articles.content_orig:
Saudi-led coalition forces fighting Yemen’s Houthis have said they intercepted two missiles and five drones targeting different parts of the country, allegedly launched by the Iran-backed rebel group.
“Air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia towards Riyadh,” Turki al-Maliki, the Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, said in a post on X early on Sunday.
He said the coalition forces also shot down three drones in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern region on Sunday.
Earlier on Saturday, al-Maliki said two suspected Houthi drones “were intercepted and destroyed” in the Riyadh and southern regions.
Meanwhile, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), claimed to have shot down an armed Saudi coalition reconnaissance aircraft carrying out “hostile operations in the airspace of al-Jawf”.
In a post on X, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Iran-aligned group was able to “repel a number of Saudi military formations using several Yemeni-made surface-to-air missiles” and that it was the fifth aircraft the Houthis had shot down since the escalation began.
At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to the kingdom’s authorities.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport, as well as the East-West pipeline and oil infrastructure in eastern and southern Saudi Arabia.
The interceptions come as the Saudi-led forces supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government also said they intercepted several drones launched towards the Yemeni city of Marib.
Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili said government forces had made gains against the Houthis during heavy fighting in the al-Hazm and Madghal districts of al-Jawf, as fighting intensified in Marib.
Al-Nuzaili said 321 Houthi leaders had been killed or wounded in 723 targeted operations by Saudi-backed forces in the Taiz, Lahij, Marib and al-Jawf governorates, and that 117 military vehicles used by the Iran-allied rebel group had been destroyed.
The coalition carried out at least 37 air strikes and 56 drone attacks, as well as 541 artillery strikes.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the Saudi-led coalition had launched 72 air strikes against the Houthis in the Saada, Taiz, Lahij and al-Jawf governorates over the past 24 hours.
He said the Houthis targeted Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces in the Kharaz area of the Lahij governorate with ballistic missiles.
Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported that two women and two children were injured as a result of artillery shelling by Saudi-backed forces in a residential neighbourhood of the Shuaub district in Sanaa, Yemen’s capital controlled by the Houthis.
More than 340,000 people have been displaced as a result of fighting in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration.
As the fight between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis escalated, the US Embassy in Riyadh issued a nationwide security alert on Saturday urging Americans in the kingdom to exercise “heightened vigilance”, citing an increased threat of Houthi attacks.
The embassy said Houthi attacks on airports and other critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia had “caused civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions”, warning that hostilities could spread “rapidly”.
“Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia,” it said.

articles.title_orig: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder
articles.title_zh: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder
articles.content_orig:
An old English proverb anchored in superstition from ancient Greek and Roman beliefs is that bad luck always comes in threes, but that does not mean bad luck was always random.
The United States has now experienced two debilitating, unprecedented blackouts across critical infrastructure in two days. The timing is almost too coincidental to be a coincidence – coming on the heels of the removal of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO amidst an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, widespread recriminations about chip exports to China, and demands for tighter export controls and more hawkish policies against China.
Could China and other hostile foreign actors be targeting U.S. infrastructure? It’s too early to know for sure, but the country deserves far more transparent answers than we have received so far.
At 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday , November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded every departing flight in America, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the third nationwide ground stop ever ordered. The first came on Sept. 11, 2001; the second more than 20 years later, on Jan. 11, 2023.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy would say only that “a communication issue” had struck every one of the 22 centers that guide planes across the country, and that technicians were investigating. A subsequent press conference by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did little to reassure anyone, with no answers about what happened and little reassurance that it would be fixable anytime soon, with airports sending travelers home and communicating that flight cancellations would persist for many hours at a minimum, if not days.
It was the second time in two days that critical infrastructure the country cannot function without simply stopped, potentially for very nefarious reasons. The day before, Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and Copilot went dark in 74 countries and stayed down for hours. Both blackouts struck within a day-and-a-half of the most damaging China espionage story in years.
The last nationwide ground stop, in 2023, lasted about 90 minutes and still delayed more than 10,000 flights and canceled 1,300 . Friday’s lasted hours with no resolution imminent on the horizon. At the four-hour point of this latest ground stop, 10,243 flights were already delayed and 3,234 cancelled, with flights grounded not only at single regional airports but across the entire nation, suggesting systemic breakdowns rather than localized issues.
Microsoft’s failure began at 11:17 a.m. ET on Thursday and spread across 19 Microsoft 365 services . Within an hour, complaints about Outlook were running at more than 2,000 times their normal level . Microsoft counts more than 450 million paid commercial seats , with many millions of those users locked out entirely from their inboxes and other critical services.
The casualty list reads like a roll call of essential services: the U.S. House of Representatives was substantively incapacitated; a federal appeals court that could not send or receive email; Britain’s Parliament and its National Health Service, where the failure threatened patients’ prescriptions; Australia’s spy agency and federal police were sent offline as well.
When a botched CrowdStrike update crashed 8.5 million machines in 2024, the Fortune 500 alone lost an estimated $5.4 billion . One risk adviser already puts Microsoft’s bill in the billions for Australia alone , not to mention the lost economic value in the U.S. or the rest of the world. This was the first time in history so many users were locked out for so long – with shifting and unsatisfactory explanations. Similarly, this is the first time in global aviation history where there has been a nationwide ground stop with no satisfactory, clear explanation and immediate fix.
Microsoft wrote the playbook for false comfort. For a full day it insisted there was “no indication” of malicious activity while its own bulletins showed it did not know what had broken. If it did not know for sure, then how could they know for sure there was no indication of anything malicious amidst shifting explanations?
First it blamed elevated load, then servers that had unexpectedly dropped out . It found no recent change that lined up with the failure. Hours later, it was rolling back a network change that did . Early Friday, engineers were still trying to “pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx.”
Only on Friday afternoon did Microsoft name a culprit : a flaw introduced during a network capacity upgrade, “not related to cyber.” That sequence is as nonsensical as it is falsely reassuring. No patient would trust a doctor who swears it is not an infection before he can diagnose the fever. You cannot rule out what you cannot yet explain, and nobody can feel particularly reassured from this disturbing sequence of events and shifting explanations.
On Thursday morning, Nvidia, whose board failures we dissected in Fortune this week , announced the resignation of Jensen Huang , the chip industry’s loudest advocate for selling to China, after he admitted an affair with a businesswoman U.S. officials suspect of spying for Beijing . Beijing has been vocal in calling it a smear amidst a rapid escalation of U.S.-China tensions. Lawmakers in both parties are demanding testimony and tighter export controls . Within three hours, inboxes went dark from Capitol Hill to Canberra. A day later, planes stopped and were grounded.
Could that really be a coincidence?
Perhaps we are being too conspiratorial, but there is a certain uncanny resemblance to Beijing’s favorite playbook, which is to divert from negative news stories by shutting down internet services and diverting public attention.
For example, in 2011, a petition to free Ai Weiwei got Change.org knocked offline . In 2012, exposés of the family fortunes of Xi Jinping and Wen Jiabao got Bloomberg and The New York Times blocked in China and targeted by hackers . In 2014, as Hong Kong marched for democracy, a newspaper and a voting site were buried under one of the largest attacks the internet had ever seen . In 2015, China’s “Great Cannon” hammered GitHub for days for hosting banned news. In 2019, Telegram and the LIHKG forum were swamped as Hong Kong marched again. In 2022, news of the zero-COVID protests on Twitter drowned in a deluge of spam . Maybe this pattern of untimely hacks was merely a coincidence – or could it have been more than coincidence?
Microsoft knows this adversary better than anyone. Hackers tied to Beijing tore through its customers’ Exchange servers in 2021 and stole some 60,000 State Department emails through its cloud in 2023, a breach a federal review board blamed on a “cascade of security failures” at Microsoft. Just three weeks ago, Microsoft itself said a China-aligned group had turned AI agents loose on more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 customers .
Whatever the cause, the lesson is identical. Some cyber experts are warning about potentially economically destabilizing cyberattacks, with researchers warning that AI-enabled hacking is spreading like a virus: attacks on previously unknown flaws have roughly doubled since capable open-source models arrived.
U.S. agencies say China’s Volt Typhoon hackers have already burrowed into American communications, transportation, energy and water networks , in some cases for five years, positioning themselves to disrupt them. They sat inside one small Massachusetts electric and water utility for more than 300 days . If the inbox and the skies can go dark on consecutive days, why not the grid, or the tap? Is it time for every business and household to buy storage batteries, water tanks, MREs and porta potties?
Of course, regardless of whether this was a Chinese or foreign malevolent actor attack, or whether it was merely the coincidental degradation of antiquated and outdated infrastructure systems, all of this takes place against the backdrop of the substantive hollowing out of U.S. government cou

articles.title_orig: FAA was warned for years about repair risks leading to nationwide ground stop
articles.title_zh: FAA was warned for years about repair risks leading to nationwide ground stop
articles.content_orig:
Even though the skies are back to being busy, some people at the Sacramento International Airport are still struggling to catch a flight, more than a day after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop order.
Thousands of travelers were left uncertain if their flight would depart on time — or at all. Others worried that while their first flight may eventually depart, it would be too late to make a connecting fligt.
"It was going to be an overnight from Portland to Miami. But I'm going to miss the flight if this flight doesn't go out," said Debbie Winter, a delayed traveler.
Other travelers were fortunate enough to avoid getting caught up in the cancellation chaos.
"We were playing a basketball tournament over at Chico State, and we got really nervous," Anthony Canales, a member of a basketball team flying back to Washington, said. "Would have been like a 12-hour drive back to Bellingham, Washington, where we're from."
Employees at car rentals near the airport said they were incredibly busy, as many travelers cut their losses and decided to drive instead.
"Either way, I was going to rent a car, but already be in Santa Rosa. So, all right, so I'm going to enjoy a two-hour drive to Santa Rosa now, getting to know the the area," said Javier Guillen, who decided to eschew his flight to drive a rental instead.
He was just one passenger on one of the thousands of flights that were either delayed or cancelled.
U.S Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy held a press conference Saturday morning, and said that the grounding was done for passenger safety.
"We shut down the airspace and we do it safely.  We get you on the ground and then we work on isolating the problem and then opening the airspace back up, which is what we did yesterday," Duffy said during the press conference.
As airlines and airports are still struggling to recover, travelers remain uncertain — but are still taking it all in stride.
"I didn't see a lot of people pissed off. It was like, okay, let's just kind of go with the flow," Guillen said.
According to the transportation department, travelers who have their flight cancelled are guaranteed a refund from the airline, regardless of what kind of ticket was purchased. Alternatively, passengers can get a penalty-free rebooking for a different flights.
If a domestic flight is delayed by more than three hours, travelers are eligible for a refund, according to the department. However, if they choose to wait out the delay, they are not eligible for any recourse.
There are already hundreds of flights tomorrow that have been canceled, as well as numerous delays.

articles.title_orig: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
articles.title_zh: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
articles.content_orig:
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings
The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this week as world leaders fly in for back-to-back high-level summits against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.
Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections .
The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy .
Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.
Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.
“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”
Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines , starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.
While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.
Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea , where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.
The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.
For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.
The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.
Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.
Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.
“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.
Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.
China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.
Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas . Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.
A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore .
Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration . Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.
Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine war briefing: US proposes Kyiv cede land to Russia for Nato membership, Zelenskyy says
articles.title_zh: Ukraine war briefing: US proposes Kyiv cede land to Russia for Nato membership, Zelenskyy says
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian president says Kyiv not ready to concede Donbas but would put idea to a referendum in exchange for security guarantees and funding. What we know on day 1,726
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US has asked for the first time if Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the eastern Donbas region that Russia does not control in exchange for Ukraine becoming a Nato member . But the Ukrainian president said his country would not surrender territory. “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’,” he said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday. “That is why ⁠I believe Nato is back on the agenda.” But he said the suggestion, which would form part of a new postwar security framework for Europe, could allow Russia to weaken Nato and reshape borders. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded ​Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a ‌national referendum. Echoing comments ‌made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, Zelenskyy dismissed Russia’s call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are ‌agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine. “We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first,” he said.
The Ukrainian president has also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality , something that could only happen if the country’s constitution was changed. “If Putin expects Ukraine’s neutrality to be enshrined, that’s not going to happen,” he said. “We’re not in Nato right now anyway.”
US President ⁠Donald Trump’s ⁠envoy and ​son-in-law Jared ⁠Kushner said on ⁠Saturday ​the US ‌was ‌focused on ‌facilitating direct engagement between Russia and ‌European nations on ​the Ukraine war , ⁠after trilateral meetings ​involving Washington, ​Moscow ​and ​Kyiv ‌this ​week. However, Washington and Nato have not yet commented on the suggestion of a swap of the Donbas for Ukraine Nato membership. Negotiations did, however, lead to agreements that European countries would join future talks on ending the war.
Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of not telling the truth over restrictions to Ukraine’s Starshield satellite system , saying the decision to impose speed limits appears to be “political” rather than “technical”. Speaking on Friday, Ukraine’s president said the restrictions affecting Ukrainian drones, in place for five days, meant they could no longer intercept incoming jet-powered Russian Shahed drones. Ukraine suspects the slowdown is a deliberate US tactic, designed to put pressure on Zelenskyy to make concessions to Putin.
French President Emmanuel Macron said Saturday that countries seeking to limit aid to Ukraine want to impose an “unjust peace” and warned that it was a recipe for another war . “Those who want to ration aid to Ukraine wish underneath it all to force an unjust peace on it” and, by extension, all of Europe, Macron said on social media. “That is a recipe for another war. That cannot be France’s position.”
Russian forces ⁠struck a cargo vessel in ⁠the ⁠Ukrainian ​port of Chornomorsk , RIA ⁠news agency cited the Russian ⁠defence ministry ​as ‌saying on ‌Saturday. The ministry ‌said the ship was being used to supply the Ukrainian ‌military. Meanwhile, Ukrainian strikes on the Samara oil pipeline station near the village of Prosvet in Russia’s Samara region on Friday set several oil storage tanks on fire, Ukraine’s General Staff said. The facility is a key part of the network exporting Russian oil to global markets, the General Staff said. Separately, 22 people were injured in a Russian attack on the south-east Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Friday, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said.

articles.title_orig: The world according to China
articles.title_zh: The world according to China
articles.content_orig:
X i Jinping spoke with unusual candor about the international situation at the start of China’s recent National People’s Congress. According to him, “Western countries — led by the U.S. — have implemented all-round containment, encirclement, and suppression against us,” and this campaign is “bringing unprecedentedly severe challenges to our country’s development.”
He forgot to mention that his own actions have caused this backlash. China’s belligerence is increasingly alarming its neighbors, who are drawing close to each other and to the U.S. for protection. To counter them, Xi is trying to centralize his control over China and make gains in Europe and the Middle East. The question is if China’s neighbors can build up defenses faster than China can break through them. And so far, the signs are not encouraging.
Mike Watson was the deputy director of the Center for Strategy and American Statecraft at the Hudson Institute.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town
articles.content_orig:
On a visit to an isolated Andean village in his former diocese, Pope Leo XIV has spoken about the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future", which he said had left communities under threat.
About 6,000 people live in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, which is located in a remote part of the Andes mountains in northern Peru, but the Pope's visit drew a crowd of about 20,000, according to the Vatican.
At an outdoor Mass, Pope Leo spoke of "declining birth rates that are emptying villages," and the unequal distribution of the land's resources.
Over 40% of the population in the Cajamarca region, where the town is located, live in poverty - the highest figure in Peru, according to official data.
Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.
In his sermon, Pope Leo thanked those who had made the journey to him and emphasised the importance of never losing heart, despite life's difficulties.
Santa Cruz is within the Diocese of Chiclayo, where Pope Leo served as bishop from 2015 to 2023. During his tenure, he visited Santa Cruz several times a year to minister to the town's rural population.
On Saturday he returned by helicopter, where he was greeted by singing and cheering. He later did a tour in a popemobile, where he waved to people who had travelled from across the region to see him.
Speaking at a local parish on Saturday, the Pope said he felt "joy" at being able to visit the small town once again.
"It is like a very big dream that the Lord has allowed this servant to come here," he said.
Rev. Kevin Noriega, who was ordained in 2018 by the then-bishop, told Reuters the visit had brought "enormous hope and emotion" to Santa Cruz.
He said: "People are eager to experience this Holy Mass ... because after so much time they will be able to see their bishop - 'Father Robert,' as they used to call him - now as the Holy Father."
Peru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the leader of the Catholic church, who was elected in May 2025.
The 12-day trip has included stops in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in Peru carries personal significance.
The US-born pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.
The pontiff is set to leave Chiclayo on Sunday, when he will head to Cusco, and then on to a Peruvian sector of the Amazon rainforest. His tour of the region will conclude on Monday, at which point Pope Leo will return to Rome.

articles.title_orig: 18 Years After Mumbai Massacre, Man Arrested for Spying on Chabad
articles.title_zh: 18 Years After Mumbai Massacre, Man Arrested for Spying on Chabad
articles.content_orig:
Nearly 18 years after the deadly terrorist attack on Mumbai’s Chabad House, India arrested a 20-year-old man suspected of gathering intelligence on the building. Full Story
Nearly 18 years after the deadly terrorist attack on Mumbai’s Chabad House, India arrested a 20-year-old man suspected of gathering intelligence on the building. Full Story
Indian authorities have arrested a 20-year-old man suspected of conducting surveillance of the Chabad House in Mumbai, nearly 18 years after the devastating terrorist attack that claimed the lives of Shluchim Rabbi Gabi and Rivky Holtzberg , HYD.
The suspect, identified as Yash Singh , a resident of Airoli in Navi Mumbai, was arrested on Saturday, November 14, following intelligence reports suggesting he was gathering sensitive information about Jewish institutions and individuals on behalf of foreign handlers.
According to Indian news outlets, including NDTV and The Times of India, Singh allegedly photographed sensitive locations, collected vehicle details and gathered precise geographical information about Jewish residents, businesses and foreign nationals in Mumbai.
The investigation reportedly began after Maharashtra’s Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) received information about Singh’s suspected connections to international criminal networks through social media.
Singh was initially detained by the ATS and subsequently arrested by police from the southern Indian state of Kerala in connection with an existing investigation under India’s Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
According to Indian police, Singh was allegedly instructed to conduct reconnaissance of sensitive locations in Mumbai, particularly the Chabad House, also known as Nariman House, in the Colaba neighborhood.
Investigators suspect that he received payments for gathering information and communicating with handlers connected to criminal and extremist networks overseas.
The reported surveillance has raised particular concern because of its similarities to the intelligence-gathering operations that preceded the November 2008 Mumbai terrorist attacks.
Months before those attacks, David Headley , a Pakistani-American operative working with the Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist organization, conducted extensive reconnaissance of potential targets in Mumbai, including the Chabad House. His surveillance helped the terrorists plan their deadly assault.
On November 26, 2008, terrorists launched coordinated attacks across Mumbai, killing 166 people over three days.
At the Chabad House, terrorists murdered Rabbi and Mrs. Holtzberg, along with four Jewish visitors. The Holtzbergs’ two-year-old son, Moshe , survived after his Indian nanny, Sandra Samuels , courageously rescued him from the building. He was subsequently brought to Israel.
The latest arrest comes less than two weeks before the 18th anniversary of the massacre.
In response to the reports, Chabad’s CWA Emergency and Security Center is calling on Shluchim around the world to increase their vigilance and review security precautions at their Chabad Houses.
“This report reminds us just how much vigilance can save lives,” the organization said.
The warning follows a security presentation at the International Kinus Hashluchim, where thousands of Shluchim watched a special video during Thursday night’s general session highlighting Chabad’s efforts to protect Shluchim and Chabad Houses around the world.
The presentation emphasized the importance of implementing security measures at Chabad institutions.
Indian authorities are continuing their investigation into Singh’s alleged connections with foreign networks. Investigators have not publicly established that the suspect was involved in planning a specific attack against the Chabad House.

articles.title_zh: IRS raises 401(k) contribution limit by $1,000 for 2027 as retirement savings caps increase
articles.content_orig:
The 2027 contribution limit for 401(k) plans is rising to $25,500, up $1,000 from 2026’s $24,500 cap.
The IRS has increased the amount workers can contribute to their 401(k) , up $1,000 from last year.
The government inflation-adjusted the 2027 limit to $25,500, a boost from 2026’s $24,500 limit, according to a recent IRS release.
"Along with the Working Families Tax Cuts, this increase in the pension limitations will help American families keep more of their hard-earned income," IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement.
"With the new adjustment in place now, the IRS is giving taxpayers and employers the information needed to make retirement planning decisions for the year ahead."
AMERICA’S RETIREMENT SYSTEM IS BROKEN. TRUMP MAY HAVE FOUND A BOLD FIX
The IRS has increased the amount workers can contribute to their 401(k), up $1,000 from last year. (Getty iStock / Getty Images)
The limit for Individual Retirement Account (IRA) accounts will remain at $7,500.
For people 50 and over, the IRA catch-up contribution limit remains at $1,100. It was amended under the SECURE Act of 2022 to include an annual cost-of-living adjustment, according to the IRS.
The catch-up contribution limit for workers 50 and over with a 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans or the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan has gone up by $500 to $8,500.

The catch-up contribution limit that generally applies to employees aged 50 and over who participate in most 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $8,500, up from $8,000 for 2026.
And people 50 and over with most of those plans will be able to contribute up to $34,000 each year starting next year.

articles.title_orig: Biden Reveals What Angela Merkel Really Thought of Donald Trump
articles.title_zh: Biden Reveals What Angela Merkel Really Thought of Donald Trump
articles.content_orig:
Former President Joe Biden has shared Angela Merkel 's private views of Donald Trump in his new memoir , revealing what the former German chancellor told him behind closed doors.
In excerpts shared with Newsweek from Biden's forthcoming White House memoir, Promise Me, America , the former president recalls how Merkel candidly discussed her difficult relationship with Trump during their early conversations after he entered the White House in January 2021.
The former German chancellor described Trump as "emotional," and questioned his fascination with Russian President Vladimir Putin and other authoritarian leaders, Biden writes in the memoir.
Biden writes that Merkel was particularly frustrated by Trump's behavior during their meetings, including his refusal to shake her hand, and his apparent preference for personal impulses over established facts.
"In our conversations... Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts," Biden writes.
"She also wondered why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel."
The revelations offer a glimpse into the private conversations Biden held with one of Europe's most influential leaders as he sought to rebuild relations with traditional American allies following four years of Trump's "America First" foreign policy.
Newsweek has reached out to Merkel and the White House for comment.
Merkel's relationship with Trump was frequently strained throughout his first presidency, with disagreements extending beyond their personal interactions to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's energy relationship with Russia.
One of their most memorable encounters came during Merkel's first Oval Office visit in March 2017.
Photographers captured an awkward moment when the two leaders sat alongside each other and were repeatedly encouraged to shake hands. Merkel turned toward Trump and quietly asked, "Do you want to have a handshake?"
Trump did not respond, remaining seated with his hands clasped as cameras continued taking photographs.
Merkel also reflected on the encounter in her 2024 memoir, Freedom , writing that she had initially approached Trump as though he were "someone completely normal." She described their interactions as feeling like "a competition: you or me."
Their disagreements also became increasingly public.
Trump repeatedly criticized Germany for failing to meet NATO's defense-spending target of 2 percent of gross domestic product, accusing Berlin of not contributing enough to the alliance and threatening to reconsider America's commitment to NATO.
He also threatened tariffs on German automotive exports and criticized Germany's support for the Nord Stream 2 natural gas pipeline, arguing that Berlin was making itself too dependent on Russian energy.
Merkel, meanwhile, opposed Trump's decisions to withdraw the United States from the 2015 Paris Climate Accord and the Iran nuclear deal.
Following a contentious G7 summit in Sicily in 2017, she warned that Europe could no longer completely rely on others.
"The times in which we could completely depend on others are, to a certain extent, over," Merkel said.
Her comments reflected growing concern among European leaders about the reliability of the transatlantic relationship under Trump.
Biden's conversations with Merkel formed part of a broader effort to restore confidence among American allies when he took office in January 2021.
In Promise Me, America , he describes how he worked to reassure European leaders that Washington would once again engage with international institutions and traditional partners.
Merkel, who had served as German chancellor since 2005, was approaching the end of her 16-year tenure. During Trump's presidency, she had increasingly become a central figure in European discussions about the future of the Western alliance.
Biden writes that restoring those relationships was a priority, particularly as tensions with Russia continued to grow.
His account of Merkel's concerns about Putin is particularly notable given the developments that followed.
Biden reveals that U.S. intelligence agencies were tracking increasingly concerning Russian military movements around Ukraine throughout 2021, months before Putin launched his full-scale invasion in February 2022.
He writes that he initially struggled to convince European allies, NATO members and Ukrainian officials that Putin was preparing to invade the entire country rather than pursue a more limited operation in the Donbas region.
The president eventually shared intelligence about Russian plans for a coup in Kyiv, including preparations for a propaganda video that he describes as an elaborate, almost "Hollywood production" designed to manufacture a pretext for an invasion.
Biden also recounts dispatching CIA Director Bill Burns to Moscow in November 2021 and personally confronting Putin in a phone call on December 7.
Merkel is among several international figures who feature prominently in Biden's retrospective of his presidency.
The memoir also contains candid accounts of his dealings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, whom Biden initially questioned whether he had the experience and resilience to withstand a full-scale military crisis.
Although Biden ultimately praised Zelensky's wartime leadership, he wrote they sometimes had a strained relationship, saying the Ukrainian leader could be "moody and stubborn" and "not as grateful as I would have expected" as he repeatedly pressed Washington for additional weapons and financial assistance.
Biden also revisits the chaotic August 2021 withdrawal from Afghanistan in the book, writing that military and intelligence leaders had assured him the Afghan government and capital would remain standing for at least six months after American troops departed.
Instead, that assessment collapsed within days as Taliban forces advanced and Afghan President Ashraf Ghani fled the country.
The former president also reflects on meeting grieving families at Dover Air Force Base following the Abbey Gate bombing, which killed 13 American service members.
He acknowledges that some relatives viewed him as responsible for their suffering and that several would never forgive him.
Promise Me, America , published by Little, Brown and Company, is scheduled for release on Tuesday, November 17.

articles.title_orig: How Jensen Huang Built the Backdoor Route That Keeps Beijing in the AI Race
articles.title_zh: How Jensen Huang Built the Backdoor Route That Keeps Beijing in the AI Race
articles.content_orig:
Headquartered in a curved glass skyscraper that boasts commanding views over Singapore’s Marina Bay district, Megaspeed International is just the type of fast-growing tech start-up that Asia’s wealthy city-state has been keen to attract.
In three years, the corporate entity has gone from an inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary to one of Asia’s biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US.
But its rapid rise has also propelled it to the center of an alleged spy scandal that’s now engulfing Nvidia , the $4 trillion company behind the world’s most advanced chips.
At the same time, suspicions that Megaspeed may be exploiting a loophole in US export controls is exacerbating a rift within the US government on how to best keep China from accessing its most sensitive technologies.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting to having an affair. Congress has also called on him to testify behind closed doors about his romantic relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, whom US officials believe to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Beijing has said the claim is a “groundless” attempt to smear China.
Also known as Huang Le , the 43-year-old Chinese executive played an integral role in establishing Megaspeed, according to corporate documents and media reports. CNN has made continued efforts to reach her for comment.
But as Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia, it came under the scrutiny of the Singaporean government, as well as US officials concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers.
“Chips are the absolute ground-zero of all other technology,” said Alex Capri, a senior lecturer in the business school at the National University of Singapore. “The appetite for Nvidia’s chips in China is absolutely insatiable… Nvidia chips are still far and away the best.”
But US export controls have fettered Chinese access to its most advanced semiconductor technology, spawning a shadow industry of complex transactions, shell companies and chip smuggling – of which Megaspeed is now under suspicion by US authorities and lawmakers of helping enable.
Nvidia’s CEO is out after 33 years. What’s next?
On Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong said in a statement the company has cooperated with inspections by the US Department of Commerce and has retained a US law firm to independently verify its compliance with export controls.
“Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously. Compliance is a fundamental priority for the company, and Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government,” the statement said.
In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia’s most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China’s tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them.
US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those.
Incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, an offshoot of a Chinese gaming company, the company’s name changed to Megaspeed in March 2023, and Alice Huang became a director through November of that year. Since then, trade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia.
Capri, who also wrote the book, “Techno-Nationalism: How It’s Reshaping Trade, Geopolitics and Society,” said Megaspeed’s business model, in which it builds data centers and rents out its computing services, gives Chinese companies another point of access to advanced US chips.
“If you put me on the restricted list to drive a Ferrari, and I say ‘Okay, well I can’t buy a Ferrari, I can’t import a Ferrari, but I can just go to a car dealership and rent a Ferrari,’ right? And do whatever I want with the Ferrari,” he said. “That’s an issue. It’s the car dealership that you have to control.”
Corporate filings show connections between subsidiary entities of Megaspeed and Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba, including the pledging of collateral. CNN has sought comment from Alibaba.
In other cases, Chinese buyers have been able to procure sensitive components of their own, often done through a web of ghost corporations and brokers through which the chips – sometimes concealed in other electronics or containers – can reach end users in China, experts said.
Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year.
“This is a pipeline that has developed that benefits from the fact that there is minimal scrutiny on US air data, that you can bring things into Singapore, Malaysia, Central and Southeast Asia and then move those goods, sometimes through Thailand, into China,” trade data investigator William George told CNN.
“It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks,” he said.
Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company’s server purchases and their final destinations.
In a statement, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence Huang that had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information “to downplay her role” at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing.
The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws.
A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia.
Jensen Huang, who has accompanied US President Donald Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, has lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports. The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue.
However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well.
They include Northwestern Polytechnical University, based in Xi’an, the capital of China’s Shaanxi province, one of the nation’s leading universities with military ties, known collectively as the “Seven Sons of National Defense.”
Northwestern Polytechnical University has been on the US Department of Commerce’s Entity List since 2001, yet it bought four H200 chips last month for $250,000, according to procurement records published on its own website that have since been deleted.
Northwestern Polytechnical University did not respond to a phone call from CNN seeking comment.
Despite investigation by the US, Megaspeed has not been labeled a national security threat or subject to limitations on chip purchases — a decision by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that led to a confrontation by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
Meanwhile, Democratic lawmakers, whose party recently won control of the House and Senate, are calling for greater oversight for US exports of advanced chips, days before Trump’s due to meet Xi for the third time this year in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.
A growing number of chip smuggling cases has fueled calls for harsher legal enforcement outside the US as well. The Taiwanese government is seeking to criminalize unauthorized exports of advanced AI chips to China, as prosecutors there charged nine people in a scheme to sneak Nvidia chips into China through Japan, Indonesia and Hong Kong.

articles.title_orig: Fifth Canadian soldier dies of injuries from military training fire
articles.title_zh: Fifth Canadian soldier dies of injuries from military training fire
articles.content_orig:
EDMONTON, Alberta — A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries suffered when a wind-driven grass fire swept through troops during a military training exercise last month, the Canadian Armed Forces said Saturday.
Pvt. William Douglas Dal Bianco died Friday at a hospital in Ontario, where he had been receiving treatment since the Oct. 17 fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, the military said.
About 84 soldiers from the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were conducting attack training when winds pushed flames from a grass fire toward the troops at the base southeast of Edmonton.
The military said Saturday that 24 soldiers remain hospitalized.
“Private Dal Bianco and his fellow soldiers were training to defend Canada,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a social media post. “With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. That is service.”
The other soldiers killed were Pvt. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, British Columbia; Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, British Columbia; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.
Military police are investigating the fire, while a separate military board of inquiry will examine the circumstances of the tragedy and recommend measures to prevent similar incidents.
Carney has called the fire one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on Canadian soil.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Putin, Xi to Discuss Iran War at Unprecedented Trilateral Summit in China
articles.title_zh: Trump, Putin, Xi to Discuss Iran War at Unprecedented Trilateral Summit in China
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping will hold the first three-way meeting among the three leaders at a summit in China next week, the White House said Friday.
The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday, Nov. 19, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The Kremlin also confirmed the meeting on Saturday.
Mr. Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks and is also set to bring up the war in Iran — but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine , officials said.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.
One of the major conflicts dominating Mr. Trump's second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the U.S. officials said.
"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that U.S. envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.
Mr. Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday — their fourth meeting since the president's return to power last year.
The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.
"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," the second official said.
Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk will accompany Mr. Trump on his trip to China but will not be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.
Mr. Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen.
Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which then-U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain's Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations after World War II.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can't be enforced on others.
"It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant," Peskov said. "However, let's not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect."
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: New AI Millionaires Want Wealth Advisers Who Can Help Give Their Money Away
articles.title_zh: New AI Millionaires Want Wealth Advisers Who Can Help Give Their Money Away
articles.content_orig:
Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon on Friday that Anthropic set aside 5% of the company in a public benefit fund because AI could produce “enormous growth ” alongside “concentration of wealth”. He spoke at a fireside chat that Yahoo Finance streamed live from about 17:03 UTC on 13 November, five days before Anthropic’s IPO is expected to price .
Anthropic’s S-1/A says it contributed 846,840,960 shares of Class N common stock to the fund. At the IPO’s $70 to $78 range that stake is worth $59.3 billion to $66.1 billion, by our arithmetic, more than the $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion the base offering of 825,000,000 shares would raise.
A short explainer on IPO float, the share of a company sold in its listing. It teaches the general idea and does not discuss Anthropic’s offering or its fund.
The key insight: As we read it, Amodei pitched the fund to IPO buyers as an answer to wealth concentration, and the S-1/A sizes that answer: 846,840,960 non-voting shares, worth $59.3 billion to $66.1 billion at the range, by our arithmetic, with a board framework to add up to 2% more each time the stock rises 50%.
Dimon raised the fund about 31 minutes into the stream, saying it was something “a lot of us are probably not really familiar with”. Amodei answered: “we decided to take 5% of the company and put it in what we call a public benefit fund”.
He said the fund comes on top of “pledges that the co-founders have made to donate 80% of their wealth”, and of a program, run “since the beginning of the company”, under which the company matches shares that employees donate to charity.
On why: “there really is a worry that because so much of that new wealth is coming from this one singular technology represented by a few companies, that we could have a world where there’s enormous growth , but at the same time there’s concentration of wealth”. He said Anthropic wants to “do everything we can to counter that concentration of wealth”.
He did not name the fund’s first uses. “We’re trying to figure out what the best problems to solve are with the public benefit fund”, he said, citing as examples “making sure that the labor transition with AI goes well” and “things like biosecurity”.
The S-1/A filed on 10 November says Anthropic contributed 846,840,960 shares of Class N common stock, “representing 5% of our fully diluted shares as of June 30, 2026”, assuming full conversion of the Amazon notes, to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary.
Class N shares have no voting rights, except as otherwise required by law, the filing says; our explainer on non-voting stock covers the class. The fund’s shares “may be transferred or donated to a third party, or otherwise sold in a registered public offering or private placement transaction”.
The board has also approved a framework to add up to 2% of then-outstanding shares each time the share price rises 50% above the prior milestone, starting from the IPO price . A milestone counts only when the closing price has exceeded the threshold on at least 90 of the trailing 120 trading days, and any contribution is at the board’s discretion.
The board decides allocations until it approves a governance structure for the fund; the initial managers are Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Jack Clark and Dr. Neil “Buddy” Shah, the filing says.
Amodei described the co-founders’ pledge as 80% of their wealth. The S-1/A words it as a pledge “to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in Anthropic to philanthropic causes”.
The filing adds that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations”. It also describes the donation matching program Amodei mentioned, through which employees can pledge part of their equity awards to charity.
At $70 a share the fund’s 846,840,960 shares are worth $59.3 billion; at $78, $66.1 billion, by our arithmetic. The base offering sells 825,000,000 Class A shares, $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion at the same prices, so the fund holds about 2.6% more shares than the IPO sells, by our arithmetic.
That value is notional: the fund’s Class N shares are not part of the offering, and the filing gives no schedule for selling or donating them. Pricing is expected on 18 November and trading on 19 November, per Anthropic’s IPO website filed with the SEC.
As we read the filing, the fund is built to grow with the share price : each 50% rise above the prior milestone can add up to 2% of then-outstanding shares, at the board’s discretion, so a rising stock would also raise the fund’s claim on the company.
As we read the two accounts, the pledge Amodei called 80% of the co-founders’ wealth is narrower in the filing, 80% of their personal equity in Anthropic, and the filing calls it voluntary and revocable.
Dario Amodei, with Jamie Dimon, 13 November 2026
“do everything we can to counter that concentration of wealth”
FOR THE SHARE COUNT The fund’s 846,840,960 Class N shares were 5% of fully diluted shares as of 30 June 2026, assuming conversion of the Amazon notes, per the S-1/A.
FOR THE STOCK At a $74 midpoint, the first three milestones would be $111.00, $166.50 and $249.75, by our arithmetic; each can add up to 2% of shares at the board’s discretion.
FOR THE TIMELINE Pricing is expected on 18 November and trading on 19 November, per Anthropic’s IPO website filed with the SEC.
This story maps onto the Business Engineer framework The AI Supercycle .
The framework describes a Barbelled Distribution Economy in which “value concentrates at the extremes (massive-scale platforms and deep- niche specialists); the middle hollows out”.
As we read it, Amodei’s worry about wealth from “a few companies” is the platform end of that barbell, and the fund is Anthropic’s stated attempt to share it. The framework predates the fund and does not discuss it.
The quotes are from our own recording of Yahoo Finance’s stream, transcribed by machine and checked against a second, larger transcription model for the passages quoted; timestamps are minutes into that recording. Amodei gave no figures for the fund beyond 5%, and no date for its first grants.
The dollar values use the filing’s price range and are not a market price ; the IPO has not priced. We did not contact Anthropic for this piece. Amodei’s answer on compute in the same conversation is in our piece on the compute dilemma .
